1.e4 d6 2.d4.name: Pirc Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4.strategy: Builds a broad pawn centre on d4 and e4 and opens the diagonal of the c1-bishop. Black lets the centre stand and plans to undermine it from a distance, so the game becomes a fight between White's space and Black's counterplay. White must keep e4 defended and decide how sharply to play for an attack.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight, covers d4 and e5 and keeps the advance d4 in reserve. The knight blocks the f-pawn, so White's sharpest attacking set-ups are off for now, and it can be pinned by ...Bg4. The result is a flexible, quieter game in which White still has to decide how big a centre to build.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the knight and protects e4 without yet committing the d-pawn. White keeps every set-up open, but Black also gets time to choose, including grabbing space in the centre. A sound, flexible alternative to the immediate 2.d4 with a more modest claim on the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 to put pressure on e5 and the long diagonal. The set-up is flexible and sound, but it leaves the centre to Black, who can occupy it at once. Slower than 2.d4.

1.e4 d6 2.c3.strategy: Supports a later d4 with the c-pawn, but it takes c3 away from the queen's knight and costs a tempo compared with playing d4 at once. Black can hit e4 or take space in the centre. Sound but slow.

1.e4 d6 2.c4.strategy: Takes space with c4 and e4 together, which controls d5 and prepares a broad centre. Black can claim the centre at once or hit e4. Sound but unusual, and less direct than 2.d4.

1.e4 d6 2.d3.strategy: Supports e4 modestly and opens the c1-bishop's diagonal. It makes no claim on d4, so Black takes space and develops without difficulty. Solid, but far less ambitious than 2.d4.

1.e4 d6 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2 on the long diagonal, where the bishop supports e4, followed by quick development and castling. It is a restrained set-up that commits no second pawn to the centre, so Black takes space and develops without opposition. Sound but unambitious.

1.e4 d6 2.Be2.strategy: A modest development that prepares quick castling and keeps d4 available. It stakes no claim in the centre, so Black can take space or develop at once and has no problems. Sound, but slower than 2.d4.

1.e4 d6 2.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop towards f7 at once, but ...Nf6 hits e4, so White has to spend a move defending it, and Black can blunt the bishop or take space in the centre. Sound and seen in practice, but less effective than 2.d4.

1.e4 d6 2.f4.name: Rat Defence: Harmonist
1.e4 d6 2.f4.strategy: Puts pawns on e4 and f4 at once, aiming to develop and push e5 later, but without d4 the centre is less stable than in the f4 systems after 2.d4. Black can hit e4 or strike at the centre. Sound and seen in practice, but less flexible than 2.d4.

1.e4 d6 2.a3.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move that supports nothing and threatens nothing. Black takes the central space while White's d-pawn and knights stay at home.

1.e4 d6 2.a4.strategy: Pushes a rook pawn instead of developing or taking the centre. The queenside space gained is of no use yet, and Black develops and takes the centre with a free hand.

1.e4 d6 2.b4.strategy: Grabs queenside space and prepares Bb2, but the pawn weakens c3 and c4 and the centre goes to Black, who has an easy game.

1.e4 d6 2.f3.strategy: Supports e4 and prepares a compact set-up, but only makes sense once the centre is built and the queen's knight developed. Here it takes f3 from the king's knight and loosens the e1-h4 diagonal for nothing while Black develops freely.

1.e4 d6 2.h3.strategy: A prophylactic rook-pawn move against ...Bg4, made before any piece is out. It loses a tempo and leaves the centre to Black, who develops unhindered.

1.e4 d6 2.Na3.strategy: Places the knight on the rim, far from the centre and without supporting d4 or e4. Black takes the centre, and White needs another tempo to bring the knight back into play.

1.e4 d6 2.Qe2.strategy: Brings the queen out early and blocks the f1-bishop, which delays kingside castling. It protects e4 but neither develops a minor piece nor prepares d4, so Black develops with ease.

1.e4 d6 2.Qf3.strategy: Brings the queen out early and takes f3 from the king's knight. Black develops with ease and gains time by attacking the queen.

1.e4 d6 2.Qh5.strategy: Brings the queen out where 2...Nf6 attacks it and the e4-pawn at once, and ...g6 also drives it back. With no real threat against f7, Black gains time for development.

1.e4 d6 2.Bd3.strategy: Puts the bishop in front of the d-pawn, so d4 is impossible until it moves again and the c1-bishop stays shut in. Black takes the centre unhindered.

1.e4 d6 2.Bb5+.strategy: Gives a check that Black meets with ...c6, attacking the bishop and gaining a tempo, or with ...Bd7 and a trade. White has used the bishop for no lasting gain.

1.e4 d6 2.Nh3.strategy: Heads for f4 or g5 from the rim, but 2...Bxh3 3.gxh3 doubles White's h-pawns and breaks up the king's side at once.

1.e4 d6 2.Ne2.strategy: Develops the knight to a passive square where it blocks the f1-bishop and the queen's path to e2, and covers d4 but not e5. Black takes space in the centre and develops with an attack on e4.

1.e4 d6 2.g4.name: Rat Defence: Spike Attack
1.e4 d6 2.g4.strategy: Weakens f3, h3 and the whole king's side while developing nothing, and ...Nf6 hits e4 at once. Black can then play against a loosened position.

1.e4 d6 2.h4.name: Rat Defence: Petruccioli Attack
1.e4 d6 2.h4.strategy: Pushes the rook pawn for a kingside attack that has nothing behind it. The centre and development are ignored and g4 is weakened, so Black can simply develop.

1.e4 d6 2.Qg4.strategy: Hangs the queen: 2...Bxg4 wins it, because the c8-bishop sees g4 along the open diagonal and nothing protects the square.

1.e4 d6 2.Ke2.strategy: Gives up castling for nothing, blocks the bishop and the queen, and leaves the king in the centre where Black gains time with natural development. A lasting concession.

1.e4 d6 2.Ba6.strategy: Loses a bishop for nothing: 2...bxa6 or 2...Nxa6 takes it, and no White piece can recapture on a6.

1.e4 d6 2.e5.strategy: Pushes the pawn where nothing protects it: 2...dxe5 wins it, and White has no recapture and no lead in development in return.

1.e4 d6.name: Pirc Defence
1.e4 d6.background: Named after the Slovenian grandmaster Vasja Pirc, who played it often from the late 1940s; in Russia it is often called the Ufimtsev Defence, after Anatoly Ufimtsev. It made its World Championship debut in Game 17 of the 1972 match in Reykjavík, when Bobby Fischer played it against Boris Spassky and drew.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6.name: Pirc Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight, attacks e4 and keeps the pawn structure flexible. Black plans to fianchetto the king's bishop and castle, letting White build a broad centre that ...c5 or ...e5 will undermine later. The price is a cramped game against sharp set-ups such as an early f4.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6.background: The same position arises from 1.e4 g6 2.d4 d6, the Modern Defence, also known as the Robatsch Defence. The tenth edition of Modern Chess Openings (1965) grouped the Pirc and the Robatsch together as the Pirc–Robatsch Defence.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and castle while keeping the knight's development in reserve, so Black can still choose the set-up later. Delaying the knight puts less early pressure on e4, which lets White blunt the g7-bishop with c3 or build a broad centre. Black waits to strike at it later with ...c5 or ...e5.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nd7.name: Rat Defence: Antal Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nd7.strategy: Covers e5, so 3.e5 would simply lose a pawn to ...dxe5 and ...Nxe5, and prepares ...e5 with a compact defence of that pawn. The knight blocks the c8-bishop and Black has taken no space yet, so White develops freely and keeps the larger share of the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nc6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Mikenas Variation
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and adds pressure on d4, but 3.d5 chases the knight: 3...Ne5 runs into 4.f4 with another tempo, and 3...Nb8 wastes time. Black can regroup and stays solid, yet White keeps an easy space advantage.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 e5.name: King's Pawn Game: Maróczy Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4 e5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once and heads for a Philidor-type pawn structure. White can instead trade everything in the centre and queens, leaving Black without castling and White a little more comfortable. Sound, but less flexible than ...Nf6.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 in Sicilian fashion, but 3.dxc5 leaves Black without a good recapture: ...dxc5 allows a queen trade that costs Black castling, and ...Qa5+ only gives White a tempo with Be3. White gets the better game for free.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 c6.strategy: Keeps open both a kingside fianchetto set-up and a compact defence of e5. The move develops nothing and gains no space, so White can reinforce the centre or expand it at leisure. Sound, but slower than developing the knight.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 e6.strategy: Sets up a compact small centre with pawns on d6 and e6 and prepares to develop the kingside pieces and castle, keeping ...c5 or ...e5 as later breaks. The c8-bishop stays shut in behind the e6-pawn, while White develops freely. Solid but passive.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 f5.name: Balogh Defence
1.e4 d6 2.d4 f5.background: Named after János Balogh, a Hungarian International Master of correspondence chess, who analysed it in the Wiener Schachzeitung in 1930. It is rarely seen today, although Hikaru Nakamura beat the grandmaster Eugene Perelshteyn with it at the HB Global Chess Challenge 2005.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 f5.strategy: Hits e4 at once but weakens the kingside and the e6-square. Most books treat 3.exf5 Bxf5 4.Qf3 Qc8 5.Bd3 as a refutation, though a few players argue that it is risky but playable.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 d5.strategy: Spends a second move on the d-pawn with White already having d4. After 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen must move again, so White is a clear tempo up.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 to pressure e4, but the pawn is easily defended while White keeps the centre and Black lags in kingside development.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 a6.strategy: Waits to play ...b5 or to cover b5, but loses a tempo while White builds the centre. It develops nothing and does not help the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space and covers b4, but costs a tempo and gives up for good the chance to cover b5 with the a-pawn. It does nothing for the centre or for development.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 h6.strategy: Prevents Bg5 but wastes a tempo; the rook pawn contributes nothing to the centre or to development, so White develops undisturbed.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 h5.strategy: Pushes the rook pawn without developing or contesting the centre. It weakens g5 and g6 and costs a tempo; White develops with Bg5, and ...h6 can no longer drive the bishop away.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 f6.strategy: Weakens the e8–h5 diagonal and the e6-square and takes f6 away from the g8-knight. Black has spent a move without developing a piece, while White simply goes on developing.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Bd7.strategy: Develops the bishop passively to d7, where it takes the natural square of the b8-knight and does nothing for the centre. White goes on developing against no opposition.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Be6.strategy: Puts the bishop on a square that 3.d5 attacks at once, gaining a tempo and space. Once the bishop retreats White has a lead in development and a cramped opponent.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Qd7.strategy: Brings the queen out early to d7, where it shuts in the c8-bishop and takes the b8-knight's natural square. Black has spent a move without developing a minor piece, and White develops unhindered.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it supports ...c5 or heads for c7 but is slow and invites Bxa6, which doubles the a-pawns after ...bxa6. White develops freely and keeps the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim aiming at f5 and g4, but Bxh6 gxh6 would double Black's kingside pawns. The knight does little for the centre while White keeps developing.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Kd7.strategy: Forfeits castling, blocks the queen, the c8-bishop and the b8-knight's natural square, and leaves the king exposed in the centre where White can open lines with a lead in development.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 b5.strategy: Hangs the b-pawn to Bxb5+, since nothing defends it. White is a clean pawn up and Black has no clear compensation.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 g5.strategy: Hangs the g-pawn to Bxg5, because the queen cannot recapture with the e7-pawn blocking its diagonal. The kingside is also loosened for good.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Bf5.strategy: Hangs the bishop: exf5 wins a piece for nothing, since nothing defends f5.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Bg4.strategy: Hangs the bishop: the white queen takes it on g4 along the open d1–h5 diagonal and nothing defends the square.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Bh3.strategy: Gives away the bishop for nothing: the g2-pawn simply takes it with gxh3 and Black has no follow-up.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn and offers a queen exchange: after Black recaptures, trading queens costs Black the right to castle and gives White a small lead in development. The endgame is easy to defend, so this gives White a pull and not more.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 e5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and attacks the pawn on e5 a second time, so Black must defend it or release the tension, while White keeps the queen exchange in reserve. Black ends up in a solid but somewhat passive set-up, and White keeps a small, lasting edge in space.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 e5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and guards e4 but lets Black take on d4; White regains the pawn with the queen and gets a little more space. The queen in the centre is a target for Black's developing moves, so the edge is small and needs care.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Bd7.name: King's Pawn Game: Philidor Gambit
1.e4 d6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Bd7.strategy: Sidesteps the queen exchange, but never wins back the pawn on e5, so Black is simply a pawn down. A developed bishop and some activity are poor payment for it.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 dxe5.strategy: Wins the pawn back at once and keeps the centre balanced. White can trade queens, which costs Black the right to castle, but the resulting endgame is solid and Black defends it without great difficulty.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 e5 3.dxe5 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the pawn on e5 with a developing move, but White simply takes on d6 and stays a pawn up. Black gets quick development and an open file in return, which is not full compensation.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and guards the e4 pawn, so White builds a broad pawn centre without hurry. Black's fianchettoed bishop will press on that centre from a distance, and White decides how to meet it: the game is a test of whether the centre is a strength or a target.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops the king's knight and guards the d4 pawn, leaving the e4 pawn for the other knight to support. White builds a classical centre against Black's fianchetto, and the game stays balanced and flexible.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6 3.c4.strategy: Builds a wide pawn centre at once and gains space on the queenside, but the pawns then need support from the pieces, and Black's fianchettoed bishop and pawn breaks will test them. Sound, though a less usual choice than developing a knight.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6 3.Nc3 c6.name: Rat Defence: Accelerated Gurgenidze
1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6 3.Nc3 c6.strategy: A waiting set-up: the pawn frees the queen's route to b6 and prepares queenside expansion, while the knight and bishop are left for later. The price is that White gets time to extend the centre before Black has challenged it.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops and hits the e4 pawn at once, so White must decide how to support the centre. Black keeps the fianchetto, castling and a later strike at the centre in hand, and plays the standard set-up against White's broad pawns.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal first, where it presses on d4 and the queenside, and holds back the knight so that Black can choose its set-up after seeing White's. The price is that e4 is not yet challenged, so White can build the centre more freely.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move and eyes the centre. White keeps the full pawn centre and many set-ups open, but the knight takes the c3 square away from the c-pawn, so White settles for a centre of e4 and d4 and waits for Black to commit.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.f3.name: Lion Defence: Lion's Jaw
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.f3.background: Garry Kasparov surprised Yasser Seirawan with it at the 1989 World Cup event in Barcelona; Seirawan found himself defending a King's Indian for the first time in his life, and drew.
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.f3.strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn instead of a piece, which keeps the c-pawn free to advance so that White can build a broad pawn centre. The price is the f3 square, now lost to the king's knight, and a slightly loosened kingside. An unusual but sound way to avoid the usual Pirc battle.

1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nf3.name: Pirc Defence: Roscher Gambit
1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops but leaves e4 unprotected, and Black simply takes the pawn with the knight. White hopes to win time by chasing the knight, but a lead in development does not pay for a pawn here, and Black can also decline and play calmly.

1.e4 d6 2.f4 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once, the natural answer to a flank pawn move that does nothing for development. The e4 pawn is attacked and no piece defends it yet, so White must decide how to meet it, and f4 has left the king slightly exposed.

1.e4 d6 2.f4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and attacks the e4-pawn, which nothing defends yet, so White has to spend a move on it. The f-pawn has done little for White's development, and Black can head for a Pirc-type set-up with a quick, easy game.

1.e4 d6 2.f4 g6.strategy: Heads for a fianchetto and ignores the e4-pawn for now. It is sound, since f4 has not helped White's development, but it asks nothing of White, who can build a broad centre with a free hand.

1.e4 d6 2.f4 d5 3.exd5.strategy: Wins a pawn and removes Black's central pawn at once. The extra pawn is hard to hold, since Black attacks it immediately and f4 has done little for development, but White takes the principled course and loses nothing by accepting.

1.e4 d6 2.f4 d5 3.e5.strategy: Closes the centre and gains space, with f4 holding up the pawn on e5. White gets a cramping wedge, but Black's c8-bishop can develop outside the pawn chain and Black has easy counterplay against the chain.

1.e4 d6 2.f4 d5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and adds pressure on d5, but Black need not hold the tension: ...dxe4 gives a plain, level game, and ...d4 gains space with tempo against the knight.

1.e4 d6 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.name: Rat Defence: Fuller Gambit
1.e4 d6 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Develops with tempo: the knight and the queen both attack the d5 pawn, which nothing defends, so White must spend a move holding it or give it back. Black prefers quick development to the immediate recapture.

1.e4 d6 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 Qxd5.strategy: Recaptures at once and centralises the queen. White gains a tempo with Nc3, but the queen has safe squares and Black reaches a comfortable game, since f4 has done little for White.

1.e4 d6 2.f4 d5 3.exd5 c6.strategy: Offers a pawn to gain time: after dxc6 Nxc6 Black has a knight developed and open lines, but is a pawn down with little to show for it unless White errs.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece with an attack on e4, which White has to defend. Black keeps every set-up open, from a fianchetto to a solid pawn chain or a Sicilian structure. The cost is that White can build a broad centre first, which Black then has to undermine rather than contest now.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, which will press on the centre from a distance, and delays the knight so Black can still choose the set-up. Nothing hits e4 yet, so White can take space and build a big centre, and Black has to strike at it in good time.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 at once and turns the game into a Sicilian with the d-pawn already on d6. Black gets queenside counterplay and an unbalanced game. White can keep the position closed, where play is slower and revolves around kingside space rather than quick central action.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 e5.strategy: Takes a share of the centre at once and builds a solid pawn chain. The price is space: Black's pieces end up cramped and passive, and White keeps the choice of how sharp the game becomes.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 c6.strategy: Keeps ...Nf6 in hand and prepares queenside expansion, but does nothing against e4 yet and takes c6 from the queen's knight. White gets more space and a free choice of set-up.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Nd7.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and a knight on f6, but blocks the c8-bishop and leaves Black short of space. White can take the centre at once. Sound enough, but more passive than ...Nf6.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Nc6.strategy: Develops and eyes d4 and e5, but blocks the c-pawn. If Black plays ...e5, White's d-pawn gains space with tempo by driving the knight away. Playable, but White's centre comes easily.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 e6.strategy: Prepares a solid but slow set-up with quick kingside development. The pawn shuts in the c8-bishop, and once White has a pawn on d4, ...d5 reaches familiar structures with Black a full tempo down, since the d-pawn has moved twice.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 b6.strategy: Plans ...Bb7 against e4, but spends a move on the queenside while White builds a big centre. The knight on c3 defends e4 easily, so the bishop's pressure achieves little and Black falls behind in development.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, hoping to reroute it to c7. That costs time, the knight does nothing for the centre in the meantime, and White builds a full centre at leisure.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Bd7.strategy: Passive development that takes d7 from the queen's knight and puts no pressure on e4. White takes the centre at leisure, and the bishop has little to do on d7.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Be6.strategy: Brings the bishop out before the knights and blocks the e-pawn. The bishop becomes a target: once White has a pawn on d4, an advance to d5 or to f5 drives it away with gain of time.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Qd7.strategy: Blocks the c8-bishop and takes d7 from the queen's knight, so Black develops awkwardly. White develops freely and builds a big centre.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where f5 is covered by the e4-pawn. After 3.d4 White threatens Bxh6, which wrecks Black's kingside pawns after ...gxh6.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 a6.strategy: Takes b5 away from White's knight and prepares ...b5, a sound but slow waiting move. It develops nothing, so White builds a broad centre at leisure.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 a5.strategy: Stops b4 but weakens b5, where a white knight becomes annoying, and helps neither development nor the centre. White simply builds the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the king's knight, weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal, and develops nothing. White develops against a clumsy set-up.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 f5.strategy: A strike at e4 that comes too early: after 3.exf5 Bxf5 the e8-h5 diagonal and e6 stay weak, and 4.Qf3 hits f5 and b7 at once, which already costs Black time.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 h6.strategy: Prophylaxis against Bg5 that costs a tempo before Black has developed a piece. White takes the centre at once, and Black has to catch up in development.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 h5.strategy: Weakens g5 and the kingside without developing anything or influencing the centre. White builds the centre and develops with an easy lead.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Bf5.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.exf5 wins a whole piece, because nothing recaptures on f5.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Bg4.strategy: Hangs the bishop to 3.Qxg4, since the d1-g4 diagonal is open. Black loses a piece for nothing.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Bh3.strategy: Loses the bishop to 3.gxh3 or 3.Nxh3, with nothing in return. The g2-pawn and the knight on g1 both guard h3.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling and walks the king into the open centre for no purpose. White develops with tempo and attacks the exposed king with ease.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 b5.strategy: Loses a pawn: 3.Nxb5 or 3.Bxb5+ takes it, since nothing defends b5, and the half-open b-file is little compensation.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 g5.strategy: Weakens f5, h5 and the whole kingside for good: after 3.d4 the c1-bishop attacks the g5-pawn, and ...h6 is met by h4, which hits it again. Black develops nothing in the meantime.

1.e4 d6 2.Nc3 d5.strategy: Moves the d-pawn a second time and loses a pawn: after 3.exd5 the pawn on d5 is guarded by Nc3, so 3...Qxd5?? 4.Nxd5 drops the queen, and after 3...Nf6 4.Bc4 White can keep the extra pawn.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Attacks the e-pawn at once and develops a piece without committing another pawn, so Black keeps every set-up open. Black lets White have the centre on purpose and undermines it later from a distance, trading some space for a flexible, solid position with counterplay to come.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Claims d4, the square White most wants, and heads for a Sicilian in which Black trades a flank pawn for White's central one. Black gets a central pawn majority and the half-open c-file for queenside counterplay; White gets more space and often a lead in development, since Black spends many moves on pawns.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 e5.strategy: Claims a share of the centre with a pawn and heads for a Philidor structure, a solid set-up for Black. The price is passivity: the f8-bishop has little scope, White keeps more space, and Black must either give up the centre by exchanging pawns or hold e5 with a cramped piece set-up.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop and delays ...Nf6, which keeps the choice between a Pirc set-up and the Modern Defence open. Black lets White build a pawn centre and plans to undermine it from the flanks. The cost is space: with e4 not attacked, White picks his own moment, and may blunt the g7-bishop with c3.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Nd7.strategy: Supports a later ...e5 and keeps f6 free for the other knight, so Black can still choose between a compact defence of e5 and a set-up with a kingside fianchetto. The knight blocks the c8-bishop and the queen, and White decides which structure arises. Sound but cramped.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Nc6.name: Nimzowitsch Defence: Williams Variation
1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Nc6.background: The same position arises from 1.e4 Nc6 2.Nf3 d6, the Williams Variation of the Nimzowitsch Defence, which is named after Aron Nimzowitsch. The sharp Keene Attack, 3.d4 Bg4 4.d5 Ne5 5.Nxe5, sacrifices the queen, which White can win back after 5...Bxd1; it is named after Raymond Keene, who played it in a 1964 game against E. Fielder.
1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece against d4 and e5, but blocks the c-pawn and can be driven back by d4-d5. White can trade a bishop for the knight and double Black's c-pawns, at the price of the bishop pair. Solid but less dynamic than the main Pirc set-ups, and often an inferior version of them.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Bg4.name: Zukertort Opening: Wade Defence
1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Bg4.strategy: Pins the knight to the queen before White has built a centre. White can break the pin or question the bishop, and if Black trades on f3, White gets the bishop pair and a lead in development. Black gets quick piece play but often gives up a bishop for a knight.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 c6.strategy: Covers d5 and b5 and opens the d8-a5 diagonal for the queen, preparing quiet development and a later central or queenside break. The pawn takes c6 from the queen's knight and does not contest d4, so White builds a centre unopposed; Black's structure is solid but passive.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares quick development and castling, with ...c5 as a later break. White has the larger centre, and the e6-pawn blocks the c8-bishop's diagonal towards h3, so Black stands solid but passive.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto ...Bb7 to press on e4. The flank set-up lets White take the centre at once, and e4 is easily protected, so the b7-bishop meets a well-guarded pawn.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Moves the d-pawn a second time: after 3.exd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen is chased with gain of time, and Black has the usual queen-out game a full tempo down.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Strikes at e4 but loosens the e8-h5 diagonal in front of the king. After 3.exf5 Bxf5 White takes the centre, a knight move to h4 can chase the bishop and win the bishop pair, and the e6-square stays weak.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the king's knight and weakens the e8-h5 diagonal and the e6-square without helping development. White builds the centre freely, while the g8-knight is left with h6 as its only square.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Bd7.strategy: Develops the bishop to a passive square where it takes d7 from the b8-knight and puts no pressure on e4. White builds a centre unopposed.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Be6.strategy: Brings the bishop out before the knights to a square where 3.Ng5 attacks it at once and d4-d5 can chase it with gain of time. It also blocks the e-pawn.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Qd7.strategy: Brings the queen out where it blocks the c8-bishop and the d7-square for the knight, with no threat behind it. White develops freely, and the queen will have to move again to free the pieces.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where the e4-pawn covers f5 and the knight does nothing against the centre. Once d4 opens the c1-bishop's diagonal, Bxh6 gxh6 can wreck Black's kingside pawns.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it covers c5 and c7 but no central square and does nothing against e4. White takes the centre, while Black still needs to develop the king's knight and decide on a set-up.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: A rim pawn move that develops nothing and fights nothing in the centre. White builds a centre with a free hand, while Black still has all of the development ahead.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Gains queenside space and takes b4 from White, but develops nothing and does not touch the centre. White simply builds a centre, and b5 is weakened, since only ...c6 can still cover it.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: Prevents Bg5 and Ng5 but spends a tempo on a precaution that is not yet needed. Nothing is developed, and White takes the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Weakens g5 and the g6-square for no purpose. It develops nothing and does not touch the centre, and White simply takes the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Loses a pawn to 3.Bxb5+, which comes with check, and nothing can take the bishop back. Black has no development or attack to show for it.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Hangs a pawn: 3.Nxg5 wins it, as nothing guards g5, and the knight then eyes f7. The advance also weakens the kingside for no return.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling for nothing and blocks the c8-bishop and the queen. White develops freely while the black king stands in the centre.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Bf5.strategy: Loses a piece to 3.exf5, as nothing can recapture on f5 and the e-pawn already attacks that square.

1.e4 d6 2.Nf3 Bh3.strategy: Hangs the bishop: 3.gxh3 wins a piece, and the doubled h-pawns and the open g-file are no compensation for it.
